steps.text:
Here is a SQL CREATE TABLE definition that matches the columns in the *tickets.csv* file:

```sql
CREATE TABLE network_maintenance_tickets (
    id            VARCHAR(50)   NOT NULL PRIMARY KEY,   -- ticket identifier (e.g. “TCK‑00123”)
    device        VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL,              -- name or tag of the device
    opened_date   DATE          NOT NULL,              -- date the ticket was opened
    priority      VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL,              -- e.g. “Low”, “Medium”, “High”, “Critical”
    status        VARCHAR(20)   NOT NULL,              -- e.g. “Open”, “In‑Progress”, “Closed”
    owner         VARCHAR(100)  NOT NULL               -- name of the person responsible
);
```

**Explanation of the column choices**

| Column | Data type | Reason |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| `id` | `VARCHAR({{int:40:60}})` | Ticket IDs are alphanumeric strings in the sample data, so a variable‑length character field is safest. |
| `device` | `VARCHAR({{int:80:120}})` | Device names/tags are short text strings; {{int:80:120}} characters gives plenty of room. |
| `opened_date` | `DATE` | The CSV stores only a date (no time component), so a `DATE` type is appropriate. |
| `priority` | `VARCHAR({{int:16:24}})` | Priorities are short words like “Low”, “Medium”, “High”, “Critical”. |
| `status` | `VARCHAR({{int:16:24}})` | Status values are short text descriptors (e.g., “Open”, “Closed”). |
| `owner` | `VARCHAR({{int:80:120}})` | Owner names can be full names; {{int:80:120}} characters comfortably covers typical names. |

You can adjust the lengths or switch to `CHAR`/`ENUM` types if you want stricter validation, but the definition above will load the synthetic CSV without any type mismatches.
